chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad, from Mu'alla ibn Muhammad, from Al-Hasan ibn Ali, from Aban ibn Uthman, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Abdillah, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who sent his falcon or his dog (to hunt), and it seized a prey and ate from it. May I eat from their remains? He said: No. Whatever the falcon killed, do not eat from it unless you slaughter it.

key_terms.الذَّبْح: Ritual slaughter; the Islamic method of slaughtering an animal by cutting the throat
key_terms.الصَّيْد: Hunting/prey; the act of hunting or the animal caught
key_terms.الْبَازِي: The falcon (baz); in Islamic jurisprudence, its prey requires ritual slaughter unlike that of the hunting dog
key_terms.فَضْل: Remains/leftovers; what remains after the hunting animal has eaten its portion

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible to eat prey caught by a falcon in Islam if it ate from the prey?
ai.summary: This hadith presents a legal ruling from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) distinguishing between game caught by a dog — which is permissible to eat if the dog was trained and dispatched according to Islamic rules — and game caught by a falcon, which requires ritual slaughter (dhabh) before consumption even if the falcon caught and ate from it. The ruling reflects a core principle in Shia fiqh regarding hunting: the falcon is not counted among the permitted hunting animals whose catch is automatically permissible; its prey must be slaughtered to be halal. This distinction would have been immediately significant to the questioner as falconry and hunting were common practices in early Islamic society, and the permissibility of such prey was a matter of daily concern.
